event: Mission San Diego de Alcalá founded; Spanish occupation of Alta California begins
why_it_matters: Begins the mission-presidio-pueblo system: California's first apparatus of labour and record.

event: Portolá expedition camps on San Francisquito Creek near the redwood later called El Palo Alto; Ohlone people already living on the land meet the party
actors: Gaspar de Portolá; Juan Crespí; Puichun Ohlone
location: San Francisquito Creek, present-day Menlo Park / Palo Alto, CA
why_it_matters: The land enters the written record as an already occupied place. Over several days Fray Juan Crespí recorded visits by “great numbers of heathens,” among the “finest and best-mannered” the expedition had met; the Spaniards declined invitations to the villages. The Ohlone-Portolá Heritage Trail statement places the Puichun, about 250 people, on this stretch of the creek. Today the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe traces ancestry through Missions Santa Clara, San Francisco de Asís and San Jose and names San Mateo and Santa Clara counties in its aboriginal homeland.
note: Campsite and dates: California Ohlone-Portolá Heritage Trail Statement of Significance (OHP draft), San Francisquito Creek / El Palo Alto camp 6–10 Nov 1769; InMenlo, 6 Nov 2019, quoting Crespí (via Bolton). Puichun estimate: Alan K. Brown, as cited in the OHP statement. Muwekma homeland and mission lineages: muwekma.org (tribal site, consulted 21 Nov 2026). Primary Crespí diary (Bolton 1927) still to be read in full; the Crespí wording here is from InMenlo’s translation, not from the diary volume itself.

event: Mission San Francisco de Asís founded at what is now 320 Dolores Street
why_it_matters: Anchors the Spanish claim to the Pacific's greatest natural harbour. Oldest intact building in the city.

event: Mission Santa Clara de Asís founded at the Tamien village of So-co-is-u-ka on the Guadalupe River
actors: Junípero Serra; Tomás de la Peña; Tamien Ohlone
why_it_matters: The nearest mission to the later Palo Alto farm, and one of the three mission communities through which the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe traces descent. Founded as La Misión Santa Clara de Thamien. Later mission records (as summarised in standard mission histories) show 8,536 baptisms and 6,809 burials — the steep demographic collapse of the mission years.
note: Date, Tamien village name, and baptism/burial totals: Wikipedia, “Mission Santa Clara de Asís” (citing Leffingwell, Yenne, Ruscin, Krell), consulted 21 Nov 2026. Single-source for the published totals (tertiary summary of mission registers). Secularisation of the mission is already in the ledger at 1834-08-09; Santa Clara itself was secularised in 1836 (same page).

event: Mexican independence; Alta California transfers to Mexico
why_it_matters: Territory transferred without administrative capacity; land grants replace governance.

event: Secularisation of the missions begins
why_it_matters: Largest land transfer in California history. Restitution promised to neophytes; almost none delivered.

event: Rancho San Francisquito granted to Antonio Buelna
why_it_matters: A Mexican land grant on the southwest side of San Francisquito Creek; it later becomes the northern part of the Stanford University campus. One of the ranchos through which the farm is assembled.
note: Year, grantee, governor, and location: Wikipedia, “Rancho San Francisquito,” consulted 21 Nov 2026 (tertiary). Exact day of the grant not established in this pass; dated 1 January as a year-only placeholder, consistent with other year-only ledger rows. The diseño itself remains outstanding (already flagged in the master timeline).

event: Rancho Rinconada del Arroyo de San Francisquito granted to María Antonia Mesa
actors: María Antonia Mesa; Juan Alvarado; Rafael Soto
location: Present-day Menlo Park and downtown Palo Alto, CA
why_it_matters: The grant south of San Francisquito Creek, later encompassing Menlo Park and downtown Palo Alto, sits beside the land that becomes the university. Rafael Soto had lived on the ground; the formal grant goes to his widow after his death in 1839.
note: Wikipedia, “Rancho Rinconada del Arroyo de San Francisquito,” consulted 21 Nov 2026 (tertiary). Year-only date (1 January placeholder).

event: Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill
why_it_matters: Detonates the incentive structure of the Pacific coast. Marshall and Sutter both ruined by it.

event: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo cedes California to the United States
why_it_matters: Converts occupation into legal ownership. Signed nine days after the gold discovery, in ignorance of it.

event: Collis Huntington is stranded in Panama on the way to California
why_it_matters: The future railroad Associate’s route west runs through an isthmus where, he wrote, there were “eight to ten deaths a day.”
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Rayner ch 2). Year-only date.

event: California constitution signed at Colton Hall
why_it_matters: Statehood organised without congressional authorisation; slavery prohibited.

event: Foreign Miners' Tax enacted
why_it_matters: Extraction from Mexican, Chilean and Peruvian miners. First appearance of a recurring Californian manoeuvre.

event: Act for the Government and Protection of Indians
why_it_matters: Permits arrest of Indians deemed loitering and indenture of Indigenous children. Forced labour in a free state.

event: California admitted as a state under the Compromise of 1850
why_it_matters: Places California on the sectional chessboard from its first day, which decides the railroad route in 1862.

event: California Land Act establishes the land commission
why_it_matters: Places burden of proof on Mexican grant-holders. Transfers land by procedure rather than by seizure.

event: Congress appropriates $150,000 for Pacific railroad surveys
why_it_matters: Four corridors surveyed. Every field commander reports his own route is best; Congress cannot decide.

event: Gadsden Purchase signed
why_it_matters: Acquires the strip required for a 32nd-parallel southern railroad route.

event: San Francisco Committee of Vigilance takes power; Fort Gunnybags
why_it_matters: Private order replaces public law in the city where the Associates’ fortunes will be centred.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (repo ch 2-07). Year-only date.

event: Theodore Judah writes “I have struck a lucky streak” as Sacramento merchants back his railroad
why_it_matters: The engineer’s survey and enthusiasm bring in the shopkeepers who will become the Big Four.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Rayner, notes to ch 3).

event: Leland Stanford elected governor of California
why_it_matters: The railroad president becomes the state’s war governor in the same year the Central Pacific is incorporated. The office and the charter travel together.
note: Year from the master timeline (Rayner). Exact election/inauguration day not rechecked in this pass; dated 1 January as a year-only placeholder.

event: Jefferson Davis speaks for a transcontinental railroad days before leaving the Senate
why_it_matters: 'To couple with bonds of iron the people of the Pacific with the valley of the Mississippi.' His departure is what makes it possible.

event: Central Pacific Railroad incorporated
actors: Leland Stanford; Collis Huntington; Mark Hopkins; Charles Crocker; Theodore Judah
why_it_matters: Four merchants and an engineer. Judah is bought out and dies in 1863.
note: Verify against articles of incorporation

event: Pacific Railway Act signed
why_it_matters: Passes only after secession empties the Southern seats. Land grants and 30-year bonds at 6 per cent. Union Pacific is the first federally chartered corporation since the Second Bank.

event: Chinese workers strike on the Sierra grade
actors: Central Pacific Chinese workforce; Charles Crocker
why_it_matters: Several thousand men demand pay parity and shorter tunnel hours. Broken within a week by cutting off food.

event: Central Pacific crews lay ten miles of track in one day
actors: Central Pacific Chinese workforce; Charles Crocker; Leland Stanford
why_it_matters: A public wager, won just before Promontory, becomes part of the railroad’s legend. The labour is Chinese; the credit is not.
note: Master timeline: Ambrose ch 16. EPUB not re-opened in this pass.

event: Golden spike completes the transcontinental railroad
why_it_matters: A public work becomes a private monopoly. The Chinese workforce is absent from the photograph.

event: Eadweard Muybridge photographs Stanford’s horse Occident at the Union Park Race Course in Sacramento
why_it_matters: The first Stanford commission, three years before the murder trial that interrupts the work. The later Palo Alto series is a return, not a beginning.
note: Anita Ventura Mozley, Eadweard Muybridge: The Stanford Years, 1872–1882 (Stanford Museum catalog, 1972; Internet Archive eadweardmuybridg00maye): May 1872, Occident at Union Park, Sacramento. Day not given; dated 1 May as a month placeholder.

event: Muybridge kills Harry Larkyns, his wife’s lover, near Calistoga; a jury later acquits him of murder
why_it_matters: The photographer of the Stanford farm is, for a time, a man who has killed. The Stanford work stops, then resumes.
note: Mozley catalog (IA eadweardmuybridg00maye) and Wikipedia, “Eadweard Muybridge,” consulted 21 Nov 2026: October 1874; acquitted on grounds of justifiable homicide. Exact day not pinned in the sources consulted; dated 1 October as a month placeholder.

event: Southern Pacific completes the line to Los Angeles
why_it_matters: Consolidation of rail power; the company begins deciding which towns exist.

event: Denis Kearney’s Workingmen march on Stanford’s Nob Hill mansion
why_it_matters: The anti-Chinese labour politics of the 1870s arrive at the door of the man whose railroad ran on Chinese labour.
note: Master timeline: Harris ch 1.2; White, Railroaded, ch 7. EPUB not re-opened in this pass. Year-only date.

event: Mark Hopkins dies in his rail car at Yuma
why_it_matters: One of the Associates is gone. His widow later adopts Timothy Hopkins, who will plat the town of Palo Alto beside the farm.
note: Master timeline: Rayner ch 12. EPUB not re-opened in this pass.

event: Muybridge’s first public demonstration of sequential photographs of Stanford’s horses at the Palo Alto Stock Farm
why_it_matters: The work that makes the farm famous beyond racing is done on this ground: twelve photographs of Abe Edgington taken in less than half a second on 15 June, then Sallie Gardner running on 19 June. A rich man’s question about a horse’s gait produces motion studies that became one of several lines leading to cinema (the research log declines the “invented cinema” framing).
note: Mozley catalog (IA eadweardmuybridg00maye): 15 June 1878, Abe Edgington, twelve positions; 19 June, Sallie Gardner. Library of Congress record for “The horse in motion… Sallie Gardner… 19 June 1878.”

event: Mussel Slough shootout
why_it_matters: Seven dead in a dispute over railroad land titles. The physical edge of legal architecture.

event: Chinese Exclusion Act signed
why_it_matters: First federal law barring a nationality. The men who built the Sierra grade are prohibited from the country they connected.

event: Leland Stanford Jr. dies in Florence
why_it_matters: The university follows. Corrects the 1885 date given in some drafts.

event: Stanford Founding Grant executed
why_it_matters: Self-perpetuating board, insulated from politics, endowed with land that cannot be sold. The clause that produces the research park in 1951.

event: Santa Clara County v. Southern Pacific decided
why_it_matters: Decided on narrow grounds; the reporter's headnote records corporate personhood. Doctrine develops over subsequent decades.

event: Yick Wo v. Hopkins decided
why_it_matters: A law fair on its face but administered with an unequal hand violates equal protection. Brought by Chinese laundry operators.

event: Timothy Hopkins plats University Park, the townsite later named Palo Alto
actors: Timothy Hopkins; Leland Stanford; Jane Stanford
why_it_matters: The adopted son of Mark Hopkins’s widow, a Stanford trustee from the founding board, buys land from the Seale estate and lays out the town that will serve the university. The farm gets a town at its gate, under a covenant forbidding the sale of alcohol.
note: Orrin Leslie Elliott, Stanford University: The First Twenty-Five Years (Stanford University Press, 1937; IA stanfroduniversi009361mbp): Hopkins “purchased a large tract of land from the Seale estate, plotted the townsite of Palo Alto (for a time called University Park), and placed it on the market,” with University Avenue cut through by the summer of 1891. Wikipedia, “Timothy Hopkins”: 737 acres, plans laid out in 1887; the town became Palo Alto in 1892. Year-only date for the platting.

event: The Stanfords travel to Bloomington to recruit David Starr Jordan as first president
actors: Leland Stanford; Jane Stanford; David Starr Jordan
why_it_matters: The founders choose an ichthyologist and future eugenics advocate to shape the university.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Miller ch 4). Year-only date.

event: Stanford University opens
why_it_matters: Free tuition, coeducational, practical curriculum. First president is a leading eugenicist.

event: Leland Stanford dies during the Panic of 1893
why_it_matters: Estate frozen; the federal government sues for $15 million. The university nearly closes.

event: Herbert Hoover meets Lou Henry in John Casper Branner’s geology laboratory at Stanford
actors: Herbert Hoover; Lou Henry Hoover; John Casper Branner
why_it_matters: The partnership that will carry a Stanford geology education into the mines of Australia and China, and later into the White House, begins in a campus lab. Lou Henry will become Stanford’s first woman graduate in geology (1898).
note: Meeting year from the master timeline (Whyte ch 2, p. 43); EPUB not re-opened in this pass. Lou Henry’s 1898 geology degree: Wikipedia, “Lou Henry Hoover,” consulted 21 Nov 2026. Year-only date.

event: Herbert Hoover begins work as a mining engineer in Western Australia, including at the Sons of Gwalia mine
why_it_matters: The Stanford geologist’s fortune is made in other people’s ground, first in Australia, then in China. The master timeline already records Whyte’s description of the air at Sons of Gwalia as “notably bad.”
note: Master timeline: Whyte ch 5, p. 100 (1897–1908). Miller Center, “Life Before the Presidency”: Hoover moved to Australia in 1897 and China in 1899. Year-only start date.

event: Lou Henry receives a bachelor’s degree in geology from Stanford, the university’s first woman to do so
actors: Lou Henry Hoover; John Casper Branner
why_it_matters: A Stanford education, in the department Hoover’s mentor built, becomes the training of the person who will translate Agricola with Hoover and live through the Boxer rising and the Kaiping years beside him.
note: Wikipedia, “Lou Henry Hoover,” consulted 21 Nov 2026: “In 1898, Hoover became the first woman to receive a bachelor’s degree in geology from Stanford.” Year-only date.

event: United States v. Wong Kim Ark decided
why_it_matters: Establishes birthright citizenship, on a case brought by a man born in San Francisco to Chinese parents.

event: Edward Ross forced out of Stanford
actors: Jane Stanford; David Starr Jordan; Edward A. Ross
why_it_matters: Founding controversy of American academic freedom, at a university built by a railroad, over criticism of railroads.

event: Hoover, acting for Bewick, Moreing, signs a side memorandum with Chang Yen-mao on the transfer of the Kaiping mines to the British Chinese Engineering and Mining Company
actors: Herbert Hoover; Chang Yen-mao; C. Algernon Moreing; Émile Francqui; Leopold II
why_it_matters: A Stanford-trained engineer, working for a British firm, is the agent who helps take China’s first modern coal mines into a London-registered company. The 19 February memorandum was supposed to bind the new company to joint Sino-British management. Belgian capital, organised through Colonel Albert Thys’s Compagnie Internationale d’Orient and backed by King Leopold II, soon holds the heavier interest. Émile Francqui, Thys’s agent-general and a former officer in Leopold’s Congo campaigns, arrives in Tientsin in April or early May 1901 to advance that interest.
note: Memorandum date, terms, and later breach: Ellsworth C. Carlson, The Kaiping Mines, 1877–1912 (Harvard East Asian Monographs, 1971), Internet Archive search-inside (id kaipingmines1877000icarl), especially the account of the 19 Feb 1901 memorandum and Joyce’s 1 Mar 1905 judgment. Francqui’s arrival, Congo service, and Leopold’s share purchases: George H. Nash, The Life of Herbert Hoover: The Engineer, 1874–1914 (W. W. Norton, 1983), Internet Archive search-inside (id lifeofherberthoo0001nash): Francqui “a former military officer who ten years before had helped King Leopold conquer the Congo”; “Early in 1902, acting through de Wouters, Leopold purchased 25,000 shares.” Compagnie Internationale d’Orient and Thys as close to the King of Belgium: Carlson, same copy. The Wikipedia claim that Francqui was sent to the Congo Free State at age 21 was not used; Nash and a 1934 Annales d’histoire économique et sociale notice (explorateur du Katanga, participant de la guerre arabe, ancien envoyé de Léopold II en Chine) are the sources in hand for his Congo role.

event: Strychnine is found in Jane Stanford’s Poland Spring water at her Nob Hill house
why_it_matters: The first poisoning, weeks before Honolulu. Bertha Berner, Jane’s secretary of long standing, is present at both scenes — a fact later writers have weighed, without a criminal case.
note: Susan Wolfe, “Who Killed Jane Stanford?,” Stanford Magazine, Sept/Oct 2003, summarising Robert W. P. Cutler, The Mysterious Death of Jane Stanford (Stanford University Press, 2003): evening of 14 January 1905, Poland Spring water, bitter taste, later found to contain enough strychnine to kill. Cutler’s own volume was not in hand this pass (not on Internet Archive; still to borrow).

event: Jane Stanford dies in Honolulu
why_it_matters: Cause contested. The institution continues without structural change, which is the load-bearing fact.

event: A Honolulu coroner’s jury finds Jane Stanford died of strychnine poisoning; David Starr Jordan publicly attributes the death to natural causes
actors: Jane Stanford; David Starr Jordan; Bertha Berner; Timothy Hopkins
why_it_matters: The institution’s president, travelling with Timothy Hopkins, hires Dr E. C. Waterhouse and tells the press the cause was heart failure (angina / a ruptured coronary artery), against the inquest. Jordan later repeats that account in his memoirs. The fact of the death is not in doubt; the cause is contested, and has been since March 1905.
note: Inquest verdict and Jordan’s Waterhouse hiring: Wolfe, Stanford Magazine, Sept/Oct 2003 (Cutler); also “Murder, He Wrote,” Stanford Magazine (review of Richard White). Jordan’s own account: The Days of a Man, vol. 2 (1922; IA daysofmanbeingme02jordrich), chapter on Mrs Stanford’s death: “false rumor that she had been poisoned”; Waterhouse “stated that the symptoms… were totally different from those of strychnine poisoning, and that some form of angina pectoris must have caused her death.” Exact day of the jury’s verdict was not pinned (Wolfe: after three days of testimony, a verdict in two minutes; a 11 March 1905 New York Times dispatch discusses the verdict). Dated 1 March as an early-March placeholder, the day after the death. Cutler’s book itself still to be read. “Mr. Hopkins” is Jordan’s wording; identifying him as trustee Timothy Hopkins is my inference from the same memoir, which names Timothy Hopkins among the founding trustees — single-source identification. Jordan gives the cause as “rupture of the coronary artery,” per a Cooper Medical College committee.

event: Justice Joyce, in Chang Yen-mao v. Moreing, holds the February 1901 Kaiping memorandum binding
actors: Chang Yen-mao; C. Algernon Moreing; Herbert Hoover
location: London, High Court of Justice, Chancery Division
why_it_matters: The same week Jane Stanford dies in Honolulu, a London judge rules on the China deal Hoover helped to make. Joyce finds that the memorandum “formed the basis and foundation of the whole arrangement,” that Chang sealed the transfer in reliance on assurances it would bind, and that the company had “declined to recognize” it. He is also disturbed by the 1901 flotation. An appeal follows (The Times, 25 January 1906, as cited by Carlson); the outcome of that appeal was not read in full in this pass.
note: Carlson, The Kaiping Mines (1971), IA search-inside: trial before Joyce in early 1905; decision 1 March 1905; testimony by Chang, Detring, Hoover, Moreing in late January and early February. Nash, The Engineer (1983), IA search-inside: trial opened 17 January 1905; verdict 1 March; Joyce’s findings as quoted. The Times (London), 2 March 1905, p. 3, is the contemporary report both books cite; the newspaper page itself was not retrieved in this pass.

event: Jordan leaves Honolulu with Jane Stanford’s body; a writer signing as “Tay Wang” writes to him
why_it_matters: The president escorts the founder home while the cause of death is still being argued.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (White, Who Killed Jane Stanford?, ch 43, p. 248).

event: San Francisco earthquake and fire
why_it_matters: Stanford badly damaged and absorbs it. Assets were land and endowment, not buildings.

event: California sterilisation law enacted
why_it_matters: California performs roughly a third of the recorded US total. Law stands until 1979.

event: Herbert Hoover joins the Stanford Board of Trustees and helps install Branner as president
why_it_matters: The mining engineer, now rich, returns as a trustee of the university that trained him. Wikipedia’s Hoover biography, in the same 1912 passage as the Hoovers’ De re metallica translation, says he “led a successful campaign to appoint Branner as the university’s president.”
note: Year from the master timeline (Whyte ch 6, p. 124) and Wikipedia, “Herbert Hoover,” consulted 21 Nov 2026. Year-only date. EPUB of Whyte not re-opened in this pass.

event: John Casper Branner becomes the second president of Stanford University
actors: John Casper Branner; David Starr Jordan
why_it_matters: Hoover’s geology teacher, and the man who paid his typhoid bills as a student, takes the presidency as Jordan becomes chancellor. The university’s early succession stays inside that circle.
note: Wikipedia, “John Casper Branner”: president 1913–31 December 1915, succeeding Jordan, succeeded by Ray Lyman Wilbur. Elliott, First Twenty-Five Years, confirms the succession. Year-only start date; exact inauguration day not pinned.

event: California Alien Land Law
why_it_matters: Bars aliens ineligible for citizenship from owning agricultural land; aimed at Japanese farmers.

event: Hoover organises the Commission for Relief in Belgium; Émile Francqui directs the Belgian Comité National de Secours et d’Alimentation
why_it_matters: The two men who faced each other over Kaiping now run the two sides of Belgian wartime relief: Hoover’s CRB bringing food in from outside, Francqui’s CNSA distributing it under occupation. After the war, leftover CRB funds help create the Belgian American Educational Foundation (9 January 1920, by the Foundation’s own later account) and sustain Hoover’s Stanford collecting.
note: Structure of CRB and CNSA: Wikipedia, “Commission for Relief in Belgium” and “Comité National de Secours et d’Alimentation,” consulted 21 Nov 2026 (tertiary, but consistent across both pages and with Francqui’s Wikipedia biography). BAEF date 9 January 1920: Wikipedia, “Belgian American Educational Foundation” — single tertiary source; mark as such. Month of CRB’s formal start is October 1914 in those pages; dated 1 October as a month placeholder.

event: Lewis Terman publishes the Stanford–Binet intelligence test
why_it_matters: A Stanford psychologist puts a number on “intelligence” that will travel with the century. The master timeline already notes the deep cut to his son Fred, later called the “father of Silicon Valley.” Terman later sits on the board of the Human Betterment Foundation, the eugenics organisation that advocated compulsory sterilisation.
note: Year from the master timeline (Harris ch 2.2; Stern, Eugenic Nation). Stern’s book was not in hand this pass. Terman as a later HBF trustee: Wikipedia, “Human Betterment Foundation,” consulted 21 Nov 2026. Year-only date.

event: Ray Lyman Wilbur becomes the third president of Stanford University
why_it_matters: A Stanford-trained physician from the Pioneer Class of 1896 runs the university until 1943 and, in 1929–33, serves as Secretary of the Interior in Hoover’s cabinet — including the years when Hoover Dam is named and let to contract.
note: Wikipedia, “Ray Lyman Wilbur”: president 22 January 1916–30 June 1943; Secretary of the Interior 5 March 1929–4 March 1933 under Hoover. Elliott, First Twenty-Five Years, describes Wilbur as the trustees’ choice and a member of the pioneer Class of 1896.

event: The Belgian government presents Hoover with official documents, many on the Belgian Congo and Ruanda-Urundi, that begin the Hoover Institution’s Africa Collection
why_it_matters: Papers of Leopold II’s former colony and of the mandate that followed it are housed on the Stanford farm because of Hoover’s wartime work with Belgium. The Institution’s page does not name Francqui; linking the gift to the Hoover–Francqui relationship (Kaiping 1901, CRB/CNSA 1914–19) is an interpretation, not a documented cause.
note: Hoover Institution, “History of the Collection: Africa,” consulted 21 Nov 2026: “The Africa Collection had its beginnings in 1919, when the Belgian government presented Herbert Hoover with a collection of official Belgian documents and reports, many pertaining to the Belgian Congo and Ruanda-Urundi.” Year-only date; exact day not given on the page. Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State 1885–1908 and died in 1909 (Wikipedia, “Leopold II of Belgium”).

event: Herbert Hoover telegrams Lou Henry Hoover pledging $50,000 to collect historical material on the First World War
why_it_matters: The founding act of what becomes the Hoover War Collection, then the Hoover Institution, on the Stanford campus. The ledger already records a 1 June 1919 funding date; this telegram is the documentary starting point given by the Institution itself.
note: Hoover Institution, “About Us,” consulted 21 Nov 2026: “On April 22, 1919, Herbert Hoover sent his wife, Lou Henry, a telegram pledging $50,000 for the purposes of collecting historical material on the First World War.” The existing 1919-06-01 ledger row is left in place; the two dates may record the pledge and a later transfer.

event: Hoover funds what becomes the Hoover War Collection
why_it_matters: $50,000 and agents in a collapsed Europe. California acquires memory infrastructure.

event: The Lou Henry Hoover House is completed on the Stanford campus; it later becomes the university president’s house
why_it_matters: Lou Henry Hoover designs a house on the farm. After the presidency it becomes the official residence of Stanford’s presidents — the Hoovers’ domestic architecture written into the institution.
note: Wikipedia, “Lou Henry Hoover House”: completed 1920, designed by Lou Henry Hoover, now the official home of the Stanford president; National Historic Landmark. Year-only date.

event: Alfred L. Kroeber’s Handbook of the Indians of California declares the “Costanoan group” extinct “so far as all practical purposes are concerned”
why_it_matters: A standard ethnographic reference, from the university across the Bay, writes the people of this land out of the present tense. Living descendants, including those later organised as the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe, contradict the claim. The 2002 federal-recognition denial turned in part on discontinuous “external identification” after 1927, not on a finding that the people had vanished.
note: Kroeber’s wording is his, and is verified: Handbook of the Indians of California (Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 78, 1925; IA handbookofindian00kroe_0), “Population. The Costanoan group is extinct so far as all practical purposes are concerned.” The factual claim of extinction is contested by the tribe’s own account (muwekma.org: “known surviving American Indian lineages aboriginal to the San Francisco Bay region who trace their ancestry through the Missions Dolores, Santa Clara, and San Jose”) and by the BIA’s later finding that 99 percent of current Muwekma members documented descent from the historic Verona Band proxy list (Wikipedia, “Muwekma Ohlone Tribe,” summarising the 2002 determination). Year-only date.

event: Stanford Graduate School of Business founded
why_it_matters: The management credential formalised. Steinbeck leaves without a degree the same year.

event: Herbert Hoover is inaugurated as president of the United States (term to 1933)
why_it_matters: The pioneer-class Stanford graduate and trustee reaches the White House; he brings Stanford president Ray Lyman Wilbur into the cabinet.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Whyte). Term 4 March 1929–4 March 1933: Wikipedia, “Herbert Hoover,” infobox, consulted 21 Nov 2026; Wilbur’s cabinet dates are from Wikipedia, “Ray Lyman Wilbur.”

event: Ray Lyman Wilbur is sworn in as U.S. Secretary of the Interior, remaining Stanford’s president
why_it_matters: A Stanford president sits in Hoover’s cabinet at Interior, the department that will let the Boulder Canyon contracts and, in September 1930, name the dam for Hoover.
note: Wikipedia, “Ray Lyman Wilbur”: Interior Secretary 5 March 1929–4 March 1933, under President Hoover, while remaining Stanford president.

event: Interior Secretary Ray Lyman Wilbur, at a Nevada rail-ceremony, announces that Boulder Dam will be named Hoover Dam
why_it_matters: The Stanford president in Hoover’s cabinet attaches the president’s name to the dam a consortium led in part by Bechtel and Henry Kaiser is about to bid on. The name will be fought over for seventeen years (Boulder Dam under FDR; Hoover Dam restored in 1947).
note: Joseph E. Stevens, Hoover Dam: An American Adventure (University of Oklahoma Press, 1988), Internet Archive search-inside (id hooverdamamerica0000stev): 17 September 1930 ceremony with Governor Balzar; Wilbur’s announcement and the subsequent press fight; name restored in 1947.

event: Six Companies, Inc. is organised; Bechtel and Henry Kaiser join the consortium that will build Hoover Dam
actors: Warren A. Bechtel; Stephen Bechtel Sr.; Henry J. Kaiser; Six Companies
why_it_matters: The dam named for a Stanford trustee and president is built by a joint venture in which the Bechtel–Kaiser share is the largest single stake (30 percent, in later standard accounts). Henry Kaiser’s later Richmond shipyards sit in the same West Coast industrial story already in the later episodes. Warren Bechtel becomes president of Six Companies; he dies in 1933 and his son Stephen D. Bechtel Sr. takes over the firm.
note: Partnership and naming of Six Companies: Laton McCartney, Friends in High Places (1988), IA search-inside (id friendsinhighpla00mcca), including Kahn’s suggestion of the name and the late settlement of the bid figure. Bechtel–Kaiser relationship and entry into the Wattis–Morrison group: Stevens, Hoover Dam (1988), IA search-inside. Construction “began in 1931 and was completed in 1936” (Stevens, opening). Ownership percentages (Bechtel-Kaiser 30%): Wikipedia, “Six Companies, Inc.,” consulted 21 Nov 2026 — tertiary; treat the exact split as single-source pending a page in Stevens or McCartney. Month from Wikipedia (“Founded February 1931”); dated 1 February as a month placeholder. Warren Bechtel’s 1933 death and succession: Wikipedia, “Warren A. Bechtel.”

event: Warren A. Bechtel dies in Moscow; Stephen D. Bechtel Sr. becomes president of the family firm
actors: Warren A. Bechtel; Stephen Bechtel Sr.
why_it_matters: The founder of the firm that helped build Hoover Dam dies before it is finished; his son runs Bechtel until 1960 and later ties it to Stanford through gifts and his son’s MBA.
note: Wikipedia, “Warren A. Bechtel” (died in Moscow, 1933) and “Stephen Bechtel Sr.” (president 1933–1960), consulted 21 Nov 2026. McCartney, Friends in High Places (IA), captions Dad Bechtel as having “died in Russia before his crowning achievement, Hoover Dam, was completed.” Year-only date.

event: Frank Crowe, for Six Companies, formally turns Hoover Dam over to the Bureau of Reclamation
actors: Henry J. Kaiser; Stephen Bechtel Sr.; Six Companies
why_it_matters: The finished dam, named for Hoover and built by a group that included Bechtel and Kaiser, is accepted by the government the next day. A Stanford network (Hoover, Wilbur) and a San Francisco building firm later tied to the campus (Bechtel) meet in the concrete.
note: Stevens, Hoover Dam (1988), IA search-inside: morning of 29 February 1936, Crowe to Ralph Lowry on the crest; “I am very happy to turn over the job for your acceptance.” Interior Secretary Ickes formally accepted the dam the next day.

event: Steinbeck's 'The Harvest Gypsies' begins publication
why_it_matters: An administrative record of a labour system compiled by someone with no institutional interest in the outcome.

event: Stephen Bechtel Sr. and John McCone open the Bechtel-McCone Corporation in Los Angeles
why_it_matters: The partnership that later biographies and government profiles treat as McCone’s wartime business. After the war McCone goes to the Air Force, the Atomic Energy Commission (chair, 1958–61) and the CIA (Director of Central Intelligence, 1961–65). McCartney also records him as a director of the Stanford Research Institute.
note: Laton McCartney, Friends in High Places (Simon & Schuster, 1988), IA search-inside (friendsinhighpla00mcca): the partners “in May 1937, proclaimed themselves in business,” McCone as president and Bechtel as chairman with controlling interest; McCone and Bechtel had been Berkeley engineering classmates. Wikipedia, “John A. McCone”: founded Bechtel-McCone; AEC chair 14 July 1958–20 January 1961; DCI 29 November 1961–28 April 1965. McCone as SRI director: McCartney (single source). Dated 1 May as a month placeholder.

event: Hewlett-Packard founded at 367 Addison Avenue
actors: Bill Hewlett; David Packard; Frederick Terman
why_it_matters: The garage is real and it is not the explanation. Terman told them to stay.

event: William Shockley’s wartime operations research for the Navy raises successful anti-submarine attacks fivefold
why_it_matters: The physicist who later brings the transistor to Mountain View learns to treat war as a problem in statistics.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Harris ch 2.4). The timeline dates this only “WWII”; 1942 is a placeholder for the wartime period, not a verified date.

event: Executive Order 9066
why_it_matters: Incarceration of some 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry. Property lost at distress prices; the transfer had beneficiaries.

event: Vannevar Bush delivers 'Science, the Endless Frontier'
why_it_matters: The intellectual case for permanent federal funding of basic research through universities.

event: Office of Naval Research established
why_it_matters: Fills the five-year gap before the NSF. American basic science funding is architected with a service branch as founding patron.

event: Stanford Research Institute established
why_it_matters: Owned by the university. The ownership is what the 1969 protests turn on.

event: Stanford Industrial Park opens
actors: Frederick Terman; Alf Brandin; Varian Associates
location: Page Mill Road, Palo Alto, CA
why_it_matters: First university-owned industrial park in the US. Direct consequence of the 1885 prohibition on selling land.
note: Sources differ on authorised 1951 vs opened 1953; resolve

event: First Stanford Industrial Park lease goes to Varian Associates; Terman is an investor and board member
location: Stanford Industrial Park, Palo Alto, CA
why_it_matters: The farm’s land is leased to a company in which the university’s engineering dean has a stake.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Harris ch 3.1). Year-only date.

event: Lockheed Missiles and Space opens in Sunnyvale
why_it_matters: Becomes the county's largest employer and is absent from the region's origin story.

event: Shockley Semiconductor opens in Mountain View
why_it_matters: Located there because his mother lived there.

event: The eight resign from Shockley; Fairchild Semiconductor follows
actors: Robert Noyce; Gordon Moore; Jean Hoerni; Eugene Kleiner; Arthur Rock; and others
why_it_matters: The spinoff becomes the Valley's reproductive mechanism, enabled by California's refusal to enforce non-competes.

event: John McCone becomes Chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission
why_it_matters: A former Bechtel-McCone partner is put in charge of the civilian nuclear agency. The construction firm and the nuclear state share a person.
note: Wikipedia, “John A. McCone”: AEC chair 14 July 1958–20 January 1961, appointed by Eisenhower.

event: Planar process developed at Fairchild
why_it_matters: Makes the integrated circuit manufacturable. The advantage lives in people and therefore walks.

event: John McCone is sworn in as Director of Central Intelligence
why_it_matters: The same man, four months after leaving the AEC, runs the CIA for Kennedy and then Johnson, including the Cuban Missile Crisis. The Bechtel world and the intelligence world are, for a time, the same career.
note: Wikipedia, “John A. McCone”: DCI 29 November 1961–28 April 1965. The New York Times obituary (16 February 1991) is the standard secondary confirmation but was paywalled in this pass (HTTP 403).

event: Knight secures Tiger distribution rights in Kobe
why_it_matters: Blue Ribbon Sports invented on the spot. The company began as a Stanford class paper.

event: Fairchild opens assembly operations in Hong Kong
why_it_matters: The offshore turn in semiconductors, in the same years Knight is arranging it in footwear.

event: Stephen Bechtel Sr.’s gift funds the remodelling of a former Zeta Psi house as Stanford’s Bechtel International Center
actors: Stephen Bechtel Sr.; Stephen Bechtel Jr.
why_it_matters: The family whose firm built Hoover Dam, and whose son took a Stanford MBA in 1948, writes its name onto a campus building for international students. Bechtel himself wrote that “friendship and mutual understanding flourish in just such surroundings as the new center will provide.”
note: Cameron Duran, “What’s in a name? Philanthropic histories bridge buildings across the Bay,” The Stanford Daily, 16 November 2023: the center “was similarly named for Bechtel, whose 1963 donation helped fund the remodeling of the former Zeta Psi fraternity house,” with the quoted sentence. McCartney, Friends in High Places, IA search-inside, lists “Stanford University’s International Student Center” among Bechtel family gifts. Stephen Bechtel Jr., Stanford GSB MBA 1948: Wikipedia, “Stephen Bechtel Jr.” Year-only date.

event: Moore's law published
why_it_matters: A coordination device rather than a prediction. Sets the industry's clock for half a century.

event: Engelbart's demonstration at the Fall Joint Computer Conference
why_it_matters: Mouse, hypertext, windows, collaborative editing. Federally funded and commercially uncaptured.

event: Students occupy the Applied Electronics Laboratory
why_it_matters: Nine days. They print the classified research they find. The senate bans classified work on 24 April.

event: Police tear-gas students protesting the SRI divestment
why_it_matters: They had asked the university to take responsibility. It took its name off the door instead.

event: First ARPANET message, UCLA to SRI
why_it_matters: The system crashes after two letters. The internet's first word is 'lo'.

event: Trustees set terms for the SRI divestment
why_it_matters: SRI sold to itself for 1 per cent of gross revenues up to $25 million. Pressure produced reorganisation, not reform.

event: Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia Capital founded on Sand Hill Road
actors: Eugene Kleiner; Tom Perkins; Don Valentine
why_it_matters: Both founded by operators from the semiconductor industry, four minutes from the campus supplying the deal flow.

event: George Shultz leaves federal office to become president and director of Bechtel, while joining the Stanford faculty
why_it_matters: The future Secretary of State, and later a distinguished fellow of the Hoover Institution, spends the mid-1970s running Bechtel and teaching at Stanford. The revolving door in the power matrix is a matter of dates.
note: Hoover Institution, “George P. Shultz” profile, consulted 21 Nov 2026: “Shultz left government service in 1974 to become president and director of the Bechtel Group, where he remained until 1982. While at Bechtel, he maintained close ties with the academic world by joining the faculty of Stanford University.” Master timeline already had “1970s” (McCartney ch 14). Year-only date.

event: Niels Reimers files the Cohen–Boyer recombinant-DNA patent application for Stanford
actors: Niels Reimers; Stanley Cohen; Herbert Boyer
why_it_matters: The university turns a laboratory method into licensing income, years before Bayh–Dole.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Berlin pt 3). Year-only date.

event: First Homebrew Computer Club meeting
why_it_matters: Circulating culture, enclosed within about five years.

event: Genentech is founded by Robert Swanson and Herbert Boyer
actors: Robert Swanson; Herbert Boyer; Kleiner Perkins
why_it_matters: A Kleiner & Perkins associate, let go with payroll to the end of 1975, builds the first biotech company on a Stanford-licensed method.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Berlin ch 15). Year from the timeline; exact founding day not rechecked.

event: ERISA prudent man rule clarified
why_it_matters: Admits pension money to venture funds. The public-money leg of the capital chokepoint.

event: IBM Personal Computer development; MS-DOS licensed non-exclusively
why_it_matters: The most valuable clause never inserted. Hardware commoditises; the operating system does not.
note: Verify contract date and terms

event: Genentech IPO
why_it_matters: Biology financed like software, on a Stanford and UCSF patent.

event: Bayh-Dole Act enacted
why_it_matters: Universities take title to federally funded inventions. Answers the question Act III left open.

event: Caspar Weinberger becomes Secretary of Defense; George Shultz becomes Secretary of State the following year — both after Bechtel
why_it_matters: The “Bechtel cabinet” of the Reagan years: Weinberger from Bechtel’s general counsel and vice presidency to Defense (1981–87), Shultz from Bechtel’s presidency to State (1982–89). After leaving office, Shultz returns to Bechtel as a director and to Stanford as a professor and Hoover Institution fellow (named Thomas W. and Susan B. Ford Distinguished Fellow in 2001).
note: Wikipedia infoboxes, consulted 21 Nov 2026: Weinberger Secretary of Defense 21 January 1981–23 November 1987; Shultz Secretary of State 16 July 1982–20 January 1989. Weinberger as Bechtel vice president and general counsel: Wikipedia, “Caspar Weinberger.” Shultz’s return to Bechtel and Hoover fellowship: Hoover Institution Shultz profile. Master timeline already sourced the cabinet appointments to Denton and McCartney (EPUBs not re-opened).

event: Peter Thiel founds The Stanford Review
why_it_matters: The campus newspaper becomes the starting point of a political and financial network that later includes PayPal and Palantir, both of them Palo Alto companies.
note: Master timeline: Chafkin ch 2, p. 24. EPUB not re-opened in this pass. Year-only date.

event: Elon Musk enrolls at Stanford and leaves almost immediately
why_it_matters: The link is thin: admitted, briefly present, no degree. The later Musk/DOGE material remains the weakest tie to the land and should stay short, as already decided in the rewrite additions document.
note: Master timeline: Vance (EPUB not re-opened). The Ep8 source pack records that Stanford has no enrollment record; the “two days” story is Musk’s own account as retold. Year-only date.

event: NSFNET backbone decommissioned; the network passes to commercial operators
why_it_matters: Thirty years of public investment transferred without compensation, equity, or public debate.

event: Netscape IPO
why_it_matters: Built on Mosaic, developed at a public university on federal funding.

event: Section 230 enacted
why_it_matters: Twenty-six words. The legal foundation of the platform economy.

event: Larry Page’s Excite pitch for BackRub includes a proposed $300,000 licence payment to Stanford
why_it_matters: The search work is already imagined as a university licence — the farm’s intellectual property, priced.
note: Master timeline: Levy ch 1. EPUB not re-opened. Month January from the timeline. Dated 1 January as a month placeholder.

event: Google operates from the Santa Margarita Avenue garage in Menlo Park at $1,700 a month
location: Santa Margarita Avenue, Menlo Park, CA
why_it_matters: The incorporation is already in the ledger (4 September 1998). This is the off-campus garage the later origin story uses.
note: Master timeline: Levy ch 1. EPUB not re-opened. Year-only date for the garage period.

event: Google incorporated
why_it_matters: Their published paper argues ad-funded search will be biased against users. Stanford owns the PageRank patent.

event: X.com and Confinity, later PayPal, operate in Palo Alto
why_it_matters: The payments company whose founders later fund and run much of the region’s next generation of firms.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Soni). Timeline dates this 1999–2002; 2002 sale to eBay is already in the ledger. Year-only date.

event: The Bureau of Indian Affairs issues a final determination against federal acknowledgment of the Muwekma Ohlone Tribe
why_it_matters: The descendants of the people on this land, documented at 99 percent descent from the historic Verona Band, are refused acknowledgment because of a gap in outside identification after 1927 — the bureaucratic successor to Kroeber’s “extinct.”
note: Wikipedia, “Muwekma Ohlone Tribe,” consulted 21 Nov 2026 (summarising the 2002 BIA final determination and the later litigation): denial for lack of evidence of external identification “since 1927”; 99% documented descent. Exact day of the final determination not confirmed on that page; dated 1 January as a year-only placeholder.

event: eBay acquires PayPal
why_it_matters: About $1.5 billion. The product was payments; the durable asset was the address book.

event: Palantir Technologies is founded in Palo Alto
why_it_matters: A company named for a seeing-stone, co-founded by two Stanford Law graduates, starts on the land and is later backed by In-Q-Tel. The intelligence trade returns to the farm’s edge.
note: Wikipedia, “Palantir Technologies”: founded 6 May 2003 by Peter Thiel, Stephen Cohen, Alex Karp, Joe Lonsdale and Nathan Gettings; early In-Q-Tel investment “about $2 million.” Master timeline already had 2003–04 naming (Chafkin ch 8, p. 113).

event: Amazon Web Services launches
why_it_matters: Computing as a metered utility. Within fifteen years much of the internet runs on three providers.

event: Nvidia introduces CUDA
why_it_matters: A software ecosystem accumulated fifteen years before there was a market for it. The switching cost that holds the position.

event: Sequoia Capital hires two investors from the Stanford endowment
why_it_matters: The university’s money managers and the venture firm on its land share people.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Mallaby ch 13, p. 334). Year-only date.

event: George Shultz joins the Theranos board of directors after a meeting with Elizabeth Holmes
why_it_matters: A Hoover Institution fellow and former Bechtel president and Secretary of State lends the start-up, founded by a Stanford dropout, the prestige of the farm’s old networks. His grandson Tyler later becomes a source for the reporting that breaks the company.
note: Wikipedia, “Theranos”: Holmes, a Stanford undergraduate, dropped out in 2003 to found the company; “In July 2011, Holmes was introduced to former US secretary of state George Shultz. After a two-hour meeting, he joined the Theranos board of directors.” Tyler Shultz as a key source for the Wall Street Journal: same page. Dated 1 July as a month placeholder. Mallaby’s account of the funding mix is already in the master timeline.

event: Facebook acquires Instagram
why_it_matters: About $1 billion for a company with no revenue. Buying the competitor before it is one.

event: Theranos begins to collapse after the Wall Street Journal’s investigation
why_it_matters: A Stanford dropout’s start-up, with a Hoover fellow on its board, fails; its money came mostly from outside Sand Hill.
note: Carried over from the master timeline (Mallaby ch 14, p. 340). The timeline dates the collapse 2015–18. Tyler Shultz as a key source for the WSJ: Wikipedia, “Theranos.” The first WSJ article’s exact date was not rechecked; dated 2015 year-only.

event: Cambridge Analytica reporting published
why_it_matters: The neutrality posture collapses in public.

event: UN fact-finding mission reports on Myanmar
why_it_matters: Addresses the platform's role in the spread of hate speech. The company's own commissioned assessment follows.

event: FTC announces $5 billion Facebook privacy settlement
why_it_matters: Largest privacy penalty the agency had imposed.

event: Stanford’s Board of Trustees approves removing David Starr Jordan’s name from Jordan Hall and other campus features
why_it_matters: The university formally reckons with its first president’s eugenics. The 2020 announcement describes Jordan as “a leader and driving force of the eugenics movement, which promoted controlled reproduction based on heritage and which helped lay the foundation for later policies of forced sterilization.” Jordan Hall, named in 1917, is temporarily called Building 420. Jordan’s own 1902 essay The Blood of the Nation had opened: “The blood of a nation determines its history.”
note: Stanford News, “Stanford will rename campus spaces named for David Starr Jordan…,” 7 October 2020, President Tessier-Lavigne and the Board of Trustees. Jordan’s wording: The Blood of the Nation (American Unitarian Association, 1902; IA bloodnationastu04jordgoog). Human Betterment Foundation advertised Jordan as a member after his death (Wikipedia, “David Starr Jordan”); Terman is documented as a later HBF trustee (Wikipedia, “Human Betterment Foundation”).

event: Proposition 22 passes in California
why_it_matters: Over $200 million spent to exempt platforms from a classification law passed the previous year.

event: CHIPS and Science Act signed
why_it_matters: Public money returns to semiconductors. Act III's triangle under the name of industrial policy.

event: Theo Baker’s Stanford Daily reporting on Marc Tessier-Lavigne’s scientific papers begins
why_it_matters: A freshman journalist on the farm forces a president’s resignation the following July (already in the ledger). In 2023 Baker becomes the youngest George Polk Award recipient for that work.
note: Master timeline: Baker ch 4, p. 94; stanford-special-committee-2023. Wikipedia, “Theo Baker”: stories beginning November 2022; Polk Special Award 2023. Dated 1 November as a month placeholder.

event: OpenAI releases ChatGPT
why_it_matters: Adoption figures widely cited from an investment bank estimate rather than a company disclosure.

event: Students for Fair Admissions decided
why_it_matters: Race-conscious admissions held unlawful. What is the credential screening for?

event: Marc Tessier-Lavigne resigns as Stanford president
why_it_matters: Review found manipulation by others in his laboratories and criticised his failure to correct the record.

event: OpenAI board removes its chief executive; reversed within five days
why_it_matters: A governance mechanism designed to constrain commercial logic was tested once and failed.

event: Technology founders seated at the presidential inauguration
why_it_matters: Visibility changes; substance does not. Thiel's roughly $15m to the 2022 Vance campaign is documented in FEC filings.
